summary: The article argues that building a robust cybersecurity workforce pipeline is imperative for national security, citing a predicted 3.5 million unfilled jobs globally by the end of 2025. It surveys national strategies, especially the U.S. Cyber Talent Enhancement Act, plus school education, scholarships, reskilling, public-private partnerships, mentoring, diversity efforts, international collaboration, AI preparation, and retention strategies.
one_line: Overview of how nations are building cybersecurity talent pipelines through education, incentives, partnerships, diversity, and retention to close a projected 3.5 million-job gap.
key_facts: Cybersecurity Ventures predicts 3.5 million unfilled cybersecurity jobs globally by the end of 2025.
Jennifer Smith, Chief Innovation Officer at the Global Cybersecurity Initiative, called the talent gap "a ticking time bomb for national security."
The United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia are weaving workforce development into their national cybersecurity strategies.
President John Doe announced the Cyber Talent Enhancement Act (CTEA) on October 3, 2023, to invest in education, training, and retention programs.
The CTEA includes plans to introduce cyber education in schools from an early age and incentives for college students to pursue cyber-related degrees.
Education Secretary Anna Richardson described integrating cybersecurity into the national curriculum at a recent cybersecurity summit.
The National Cyber Scholarship Foundation offers scholarships and competitions to encourage students to pursue cybersecurity in higher education.

The CyberReskill Initiative, launched on November 20, 2023, is a joint venture between government agencies and major tech firms to streamline entry into cybersecurity careers and anticipate future skills.
The 'experience paradox' means entry-level cybersecurity positions require prior experience; mentoring and apprenticeship programs are emerging to combat it.
Women in Cybersecurity (WiCyS) and the International Consortium of Minority Cybersecurity Professionals (ICMCP) are leading efforts to diversify the cybersecurity workforce.
The International Cybersecurity Education Initiative (ICEI), inaugurated on September 1, 2023, fosters bilateral agreements to share best practices in education, training, and workforce development.
Suzanne McCarthy, an advisor on the ICEI project, said the aim is universal cybersecurity education standards and international cooperation.
AI boot camps and courses on managing automated security systems are gaining traction in educational and professional development programs.
Retention strategies include clear career progression pathways, competitive compensation packages, and opportunities for continuous learning.
